1	# Scheduling
2	
3	Schedule tasks to run in the future — whether that's seconds from now, at a specific date/time, or on a recurring cron schedule. Scheduled tasks survive agent restarts and are persisted to SQLite.
4	
5	## Overview
6	
7	The scheduling system supports four modes:
8	
9	| Mode          | Syntax                              | Use Case                  |
10	| ------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
11	| **Delayed**   | `this.schedule(60, ...)`            | Run in 60 seconds         |
12	| **Scheduled** | `this.schedule(new Date(...), ...)` | Run at specific time      |
13	| **Cron**      | `this.schedule("0 8 * * *", ...)`   | Run on recurring schedule |
14	| **Interval**  | `this.scheduleEvery(30, ...)`       | Run every 30 seconds      |
15	
16	Under the hood, scheduling uses [Durable Object alarms](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/alarms/) to wake the agent at the right time. Tasks are stored in a SQLite table and executed in order.
17	
18	## Scheduler Lifecycle primitive
19	
20	> **Experimental.** The `Scheduler` primitive and the `agents/lifecycle`
21	> surface it builds on may change between releases. Agent's established
22	> scheduling methods (`this.schedule()` and friends) are stable.
23	
24	`Scheduler` is a reusable Lifecycle capability. A plain Lifecycle Object can
25	install it without extending `Agent`:
26	
27	```typescript
28	import { DurableObject } from "cloudflare:workers";
29	import { Lifecycle } from "agents/lifecycle";
30	import { Scheduler, type Schedule } from "agents/schedules";
31	
32	export class ReminderObject extends DurableObject<Env> {
33	  readonly scheduler = new Scheduler({
34	    callbacks: {
35	      sendReminder: (
36	        payload: { message: string },
37	        schedule: Schedule<{ message: string }>
38	      ) => {
39	        console.log(schedule.id, payload.message);
40	      }
41	    }
42	  });
43	
44	  readonly lifecycle = Lifecycle.install(this).use(this.scheduler);
45	
46	  async createReminder(message: string): Promise<string> {
47	    const schedule = await this.scheduler.set(300, "sendReminder", {
48	      message
49	    });
50	    return schedule.id;
51	  }
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Lifecycle owns the physical Durable Object alarm. Scheduler contributes its
56	earliest pending task or hung-interval recheck. Lifecycle selects the earliest
57	contribution from Scheduler, other capabilities, and the host, then rearms after
58	every alarm phase. A future Fiber or MCP capability can contribute its own wake
59	time without storing work in Scheduler or depending on it.
60	
61	Scheduler's primary API is small: callbacks are registered by name in the
62	constructor, `set()` and `every()` create schedules typed against that
63	registration, and `get()`, `list()`, and `cancel()` manage them. All of these
64	are asynchronous and work inside routed sub-agents.
65	
66	Scheduler Lifecycle hooks run without ambient host context. Registered
67	callbacks are user code, so they run inside the host invocation context with
68	the Lifecycle Object available through `getCurrentAgent()`.
69	
70	## Using Scheduler through Agent
71	
72	Every `Agent` constructs and installs the same primitive at `this.scheduler`.
73	Existing Agent applications continue to use the established methods:
74	
75	- `this.schedule()` and `this.scheduleEvery()` create schedules.
76	- `this.getScheduleById()` and `this.listSchedules()` read schedules.
77	- `this.cancelSchedule()` removes a schedule.
78	
79	These methods delegate to `this.scheduler`; no setup or migration is required.
80	Agent registers no callbacks map — a composition-root resolver keeps
81	`this.schedule(60, "methodName")` dispatching to Agent methods. Agent passes
82	only policy options (retry defaults, hung-interval timeout, error routing) and
83	adapts Lifecycle's event sink, facet transport, and host invocation boundary
84	at its composition root — there is no Agent-specific Scheduler adapter. Scheduler contributes its next wake time to the same Lifecycle alarm
85	selection as Agent keep-alive, fibers, sub-agent work, and deferred
86	destruction.
87	
88	Import `Scheduler` and runtime schedule types from the dependency-light entry
89	point:
90	
91	```typescript
92	import {
93	  Scheduler,
94	  type Schedule,
95	  type ScheduleCriteria
96	} from "agents/schedules";
97	```
98	
99	Natural-language parsing helpers use Zod and live under
100	`agents/schedules/parser`. The previous `agents/schedule` path remains as a
101	deprecated compatibility alias.
102	
103	## Quick Start
104	
105	```typescript
106	import { Agent } from "agents";
107	
108	export class ReminderAgent extends Agent {
109	  async onRequest(request: Request) {
110	    const url = new URL(request.url);
111	
112	    // Schedule in 30 seconds
113	    await this.schedule(30, "sendReminder", {
114	      message: "Check your email"
115	    });
116	
117	    // Schedule at specific time
118	    await this.schedule(new Date("2025-02-01T09:00:00Z"), "sendReminder", {
119	      message: "Monthly report due"
120	    });
121	
122	    // Schedule recurring (every day at 8am)
123	    await this.schedule("0 8 * * *", "dailyDigest", {
124	      userId: url.searchParams.get("userId")
125	    });
126	
127	    return new Response("Scheduled!");
128	  }
129	
130	  async sendReminder(payload: { message: string }) {
131	    console.log(`Reminder: ${payload.message}`);
132	    // Send notification, email, etc.
133	  }
134	
135	  async dailyDigest(payload: { userId: string }) {
136	    console.log(`Sending daily digest to ${payload.userId}`);
137	    // Generate and send digest
138	  }
139	}
140	```
141	
142	## Scheduling Modes
143	
144	### Delayed Execution
145	
146	Pass a number to schedule a task to run after a delay in **seconds**:
147	
148	```typescript
149	// Run in 10 seconds
150	await this.schedule(10, "processTask", { taskId: "123" });
151	
152	// Run in 5 minutes (300 seconds)
153	await this.schedule(300, "sendFollowUp", { email: "user@example.com" });
154	
155	// Run in 1 hour
156	await this.schedule(3600, "checkStatus", { orderId: "abc" });
157	```
158	
159	**Use cases:**
160	
161	- Debouncing rapid events
162	- Delayed notifications ("You left items in your cart")
163	- Retry with backoff
164	- Rate limiting
165	
166	### Scheduled Execution
167	
168	Pass a `Date` object to schedule a task at a specific time:
169	
170	```typescript
171	// Run tomorrow at noon
172	const tomorrow = new Date();
173	tomorrow.setDate(tomorrow.getDate() + 1);
174	tomorrow.setHours(12, 0, 0, 0);
175	await this.schedule(tomorrow, "sendReminder", { message: "Meeting time!" });
176	
177	// Run at a specific timestamp
178	await this.schedule(new Date("2025-06-15T14:30:00Z"), "triggerEvent", {
179	  eventId: "conference-2025"
180	});
181	
182	// Run in 2 hours using Date math
183	const twoHoursFromNow = new Date(Date.now() + 2 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
184	await this.schedule(twoHoursFromNow, "checkIn", {});
185	```
186	
187	**Use cases:**
188	
189	- Appointment reminders
190	- Deadline notifications
191	- Scheduled content publishing
192	- Time-based triggers
193	
194	### Recurring (Cron)
195	
196	Pass a cron expression string for recurring schedules:
197	
198	```typescript
199	// Every day at 8:00 AM
200	await this.schedule("0 8 * * *", "dailyReport", {});
201	
202	// Every hour
203	await this.schedule("0 * * * *", "hourlyCheck", {});
204	
205	// Every Monday at 9:00 AM
206	await this.schedule("0 9 * * 1", "weeklySync", {});
207	
208	// Every 15 minutes
209	await this.schedule("*/15 * * * *", "pollForUpdates", {});
210	
211	// First day of every month at midnight
212	await this.schedule("0 0 1 * *", "monthlyCleanup", {});
213	```
214	
215	**Cron syntax:** `minute hour day month weekday`
216	
217	| Field        | Values         | Special Characters |
218	| ------------ | -------------- | ------------------ |
219	| Minute       | 0-59           | `*` `,` `-` `/`    |
220	| Hour         | 0-23           | `*` `,` `-` `/`    |
221	| Day of Month | 1-31           | `*` `,` `-` `/`    |
222	| Month        | 1-12           | `*` `,` `-` `/`    |
223	| Day of Week  | 0-6 (0=Sunday) | `*` `,` `-` `/`    |
224	
225	**Common patterns:**
226	
227	```typescript
228	"* * * * *"; // Every minute
229	"*/5 * * * *"; // Every 5 minutes
230	"0 * * * *"; // Every hour (on the hour)
231	"0 0 * * *"; // Every day at midnight
232	"0 8 * * 1-5"; // Weekdays at 8am
233	"0 0 * * 0"; // Every Sunday at midnight
234	"0 0 1 * *"; // First of every month
235	```
236	
237	**Use cases:**
238	
239	- Daily/weekly reports
240	- Periodic cleanup jobs
241	- Polling external services
242	- Health checks
243	- Subscription renewals
244	
245	### Interval
246	
247	Use `scheduleEvery()` to run a task at fixed intervals (in seconds). Unlike cron, intervals support sub-minute precision and arbitrary durations:
248	
249	```typescript
250	// Poll every 30 seconds
251	await this.scheduleEvery(30, "poll", { source: "api" });
252	
253	// Health check every 45 seconds
254	await this.scheduleEvery(45, "healthCheck", {});
255	
256	// Sync every 90 seconds (1.5 minutes - can't be expressed in cron)
257	await this.scheduleEvery(90, "syncData", { destination: "warehouse" });
258	```
259	
260	**Idempotency:**
261	
262	`scheduleEvery()` is idempotent on the combination of callback name, interval, and payload — calling it multiple times with the same arguments does not create duplicate schedules. This makes it safe to call in `onStart()`, which runs on every Durable Object wake:
263	
264	```typescript
265	class MyAgent extends Agent {
266	  async onStart() {
267	    // Safe: only one schedule is created, no matter how many times the DO wakes
268	    await this.scheduleEvery(30, "tick");
269	  }
270	
271	  async tick() {
272	    console.log("tick", new Date().toISOString());
273	  }
274	}
275	```
276	
277	Calling `scheduleEvery()` with a different interval or payload creates a separate schedule, even for the same callback:
278	
279	```typescript
280	// First call creates one schedule
281	await this.scheduleEvery(30, "poll");
282	
283	// Second call with a different interval creates a second schedule
284	await this.scheduleEvery(60, "poll");
285	// Two "poll" schedules exist: one every 30s and one every 60s
286	
287	// Third call with the same arguments as the first is a no-op
288	await this.scheduleEvery(30, "poll");
289	// Still two schedules
290	```
291	
292	Different callbacks also get their own independent schedules:
293	
294	```typescript
295	// These create two separate schedules (different callbacks)
296	await this.scheduleEvery(30, "poll");
297	await this.scheduleEvery(30, "healthCheck");
298	```
299	
300	**Key differences from cron:**
301	
302	| Feature             | Cron                           | Interval               |
303	| ------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
304	| Minimum granularity | 1 minute                       | 1 second               |
305	| Arbitrary intervals | No (must fit cron pattern)     | Yes                    |
306	| Fixed schedule      | Yes (e.g., "every day at 8am") | No (relative to start) |
307	| Overlap prevention  | No                             | Yes (built-in)         |
308	
309	**Overlap prevention:**
310	
311	If a callback takes longer than the interval, the next execution is skipped (not queued). This prevents runaway resource usage:
312	
313	```typescript
314	class PollingAgent extends Agent {
315	  async poll() {
316	    // If this takes 45 seconds and interval is 30 seconds,
317	    // the next poll is skipped (with a warning logged)
318	    const data = await slowExternalApi();
319	    await this.processData(data);
320	  }
321	}
322	
323	// Set up 30-second interval
324	await this.scheduleEvery(30, "poll", {});
325	```
326	
327	When a skip occurs, you'll see a warning in logs:
328	
329	```
330	Skipping interval schedule abc123: previous execution still running
331	```
332	
333	**Error resilience:**
334	
335	If the callback throws an error, the interval continues — only that execution fails:
336	
337	```typescript
338	async syncData() {
339	  // Even if this throws, the interval keeps running
340	  const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/data");
341	  if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Sync failed");
342	  // ...
343	}
344	```
345	
346	**Use cases:**
347	
348	- Sub-minute polling (every 10, 30, 45 seconds)
349	- Intervals that don't map to cron (every 90 seconds, every 7 minutes)
350	- Rate-limited API polling with precise control
351	- Real-time data synchronization
352	
353	## Keeping the Agent Alive
354	
355	Durable Objects are evicted after a period of inactivity (typically 70-140 seconds with no incoming requests, WebSocket messages, or alarms). During long-running operations — streaming LLM responses, waiting on external APIs, running multi-step computations — the agent can be evicted mid-flight.
356	
357	`keepAlive()` prevents this by holding an alarm-backed heartbeat ref that keeps the agent active until you are done:
358	
359	```typescript
360	const dispose = await this.keepAlive();
361	try {
362	  // Long-running work that must not be interrupted
363	  const result = await longRunningComputation();
364	  await sendResults(result);
365	} finally {
366	  dispose();
367	}
368	```
369	
370	The returned disposer function cancels the heartbeat. Always call it when the work is done — otherwise the heartbeat continues indefinitely.
371	
372	### keepAliveWhile()
373	
374	For scoped work, use `keepAliveWhile()` — it runs an async function and automatically cleans up the heartbeat when it completes (or throws):
375	
376	```typescript
377	const result = await this.keepAliveWhile(async () => {
378	  const data = await longRunningComputation();
379	  return data;
380	});
381	```
382	
383	This is the recommended approach since you cannot forget to dispose the heartbeat.
384	
385	### How it works
386	
387	`keepAlive()` uses an in-memory reference count. Each call increments the count; the disposer decrements it. While the count is above zero, Agent contributes a wake time every 30 seconds to Lifecycle. No schedule rows are created and no observability events are emitted, so the heartbeat is invisible to `listSchedules()` and the scheduling diagnostics channel.
388	
389	The heartbeat does not conflict with scheduled work. Lifecycle selects one physical alarm from both contributions.
390	
391	Inside sub-agents, `keepAlive()` delegates that heartbeat ref to the top-level parent because facets do not have independent alarm slots. `keepAliveWhile()` works the same way because it calls `keepAlive()` and automatically disposes the delegated ref when the scoped work completes.
392	
393	### Multiple concurrent callers
394	
395	Each `keepAlive()` call returns an independent disposer:
396	
397	```typescript
398	const dispose1 = await this.keepAlive();
399	const dispose2 = await this.keepAlive();
400	
401	// Both heartbeats are active (ref count = 2)
402	dispose1(); // Decrements ref count to 1
403	// Agent is still alive via dispose2's ref
404	
405	dispose2(); // Ref count reaches 0 — agent can go idle
406	```
407	
408	### AIChatAgent
409	
410	`AIChatAgent` automatically calls `keepAlive()` during streaming responses. You do not need to add it yourself when using `AIChatAgent` — every LLM stream is protected from idle eviction by default.
411	
412	### When to use keepAlive()
413	
414	| Scenario                                    | Use keepAlive()?                       |
415	| ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
416	| Streaming LLM responses via `AIChatAgent`   | No — already built in                  |
417	| Long-running computation in a custom Agent  | Yes                                    |
418	| Waiting on a slow external API call         | Yes                                    |
419	| Multi-step tool execution                   | Yes                                    |
420	| Short request-response handlers             | No — not needed                        |
421	| Background work via scheduling or workflows | No — alarms already keep the DO active |
422	
423	## Managing Schedules
424	
425	### Get a Schedule
426	
427	Retrieve a scheduled task by its ID:
428	
429	```typescript
430	const schedule = await this.getScheduleById(scheduleId);
431	
432	if (schedule) {
433	  console.log(
434	    `Task ${schedule.id} will run at ${new Date(schedule.time * 1000)}`
435	  );
436	  console.log(`Callback: ${schedule.callback}`);
437	  console.log(`Type: ${schedule.type}`); // "scheduled" | "delayed" | "cron" | "interval"
438	} else {
439	  console.log("Schedule not found");
440	}
441	```
442	
443	### List Schedules
444	
445	Query scheduled tasks with optional filters:
446	
447	```typescript
448	// Get all scheduled tasks
449	const allSchedules = await this.listSchedules();
450	
451	// Get only cron jobs
452	const cronJobs = await this.listSchedules({ type: "cron" });
453	
454	// Get tasks in the next hour
455	const upcoming = await this.listSchedules({
456	  timeRange: {
457	    start: new Date(),
458	    end: new Date(Date.now() + 60 * 60 * 1000)
459	  }
460	});
461	
462	// Get a specific task by ID
463	const specific = await this.listSchedules({ id: "abc123" });
464	
465	// Combine filters
466	const upcomingCronJobs = await this.listSchedules({
467	  type: "cron",
468	  timeRange: {
469	    start: new Date(),
470	    end: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)
471	  }
472	});
473	```
474	
475	### Cancel a Schedule
476	
477	Remove a scheduled task before it executes:
478	
479	```typescript
480	const cancelled = await this.cancelSchedule(scheduleId);
481	
482	if (cancelled) {
483	  console.log("Schedule cancelled successfully");
484	} else {
485	  console.log("Schedule not found (may have already executed)");
486	}
487	```
488	
489	`cancelSchedule(id)` only matches schedules owned by the agent it is called on. A top-level agent cannot cancel a sub-agent's schedules by id, and a sub-agent cannot reach a sibling's schedules. To clear every schedule under a sub-agent (and any of its descendants), call `parent.deleteSubAgent(Cls, name)` from the parent — that bulk-cancels the prefix and tears the sub-agent down.
490	
491	**Example: Cancellable reminders**
492	
493	```typescript
494	class ReminderAgent extends Agent {
495	  async setReminder(userId: string, message: string, delaySeconds: number) {
496	    const schedule = await this.schedule(delaySeconds, "sendReminder", {
497	      userId,
498	      message
499	    });
500	
501	    // Store the schedule ID so user can cancel later
502	    this.sql`
503	      INSERT INTO user_reminders (user_id, schedule_id, message)
504	      VALUES (${userId}, ${schedule.id}, ${message})
505	    `;
506	
507	    return schedule.id;
508	  }
509	
510	  async cancelReminder(scheduleId: string) {
511	    const cancelled = await this.cancelSchedule(scheduleId);
512	
513	    if (cancelled) {
514	      this.sql`DELETE FROM user_reminders WHERE schedule_id = ${scheduleId}`;
515	    }
516	
517	    return cancelled;
518	  }
519	
520	  async sendReminder(payload: { userId: string; message: string }) {
521	    // Send the reminder...
522	
523	    // Clean up the record
524	    this.sql`DELETE FROM user_reminders WHERE user_id = ${payload.userId}`;
525	  }
526	}
527	```
528	
529	## The Schedule Object
530	
531	When you create or retrieve a schedule, you get a `Schedule` object:
532	
533	```typescript
534	type Schedule<T = string> = {
535	  id: string; // Unique identifier
536	  callback: string; // Method name to call
537	  payload: T; // Data passed to the callback
538	  retry?: RetryOptions; // Retry options (if configured)
539	  time: number; // Unix timestamp (seconds) of next execution
540	} & (
541	  | { type: "scheduled" } // One-time at specific date
542	  | { type: "delayed"; delayInSeconds: number } // One-time after delay
543	  | { type: "cron"; cron: string } // Recurring (cron expression)
544	  | { type: "interval"; intervalSeconds: number } // Recurring (fixed interval)
545	);
546	```
547	
548	**Example:**
549	
550	```typescript
551	const schedule = await this.schedule(
552	  60,
553	  "myTask",
554	  { foo: "bar" },
555	  { retry: { maxAttempts: 5 } }
556	);
557	
558	console.log(schedule);
559	// {
560	//   id: "abc123xyz",
561	//   callback: "myTask",
562	//   payload: { foo: "bar" },
563	//   retry: { maxAttempts: 5 },
564	//   time: 1706745600,
565	//   type: "delayed",
566	//   delayInSeconds: 60
567	// }
568	```

570	## Patterns
571	
572	### Rescheduling from Callbacks
573	
574	For dynamic recurring schedules, schedule the next run from within the callback:
575	
576	```typescript
577	class PollingAgent extends Agent {
578	  async startPolling(intervalSeconds: number) {
579	    await this.schedule(intervalSeconds, "poll", { interval: intervalSeconds });
580	  }
581	
582	  async poll(payload: { interval: number }) {
583	    try {
584	      const data = await fetch("https://api.example.com/updates");
585	      await this.processUpdates(await data.json());
586	    } catch (error) {
587	      console.error("Polling failed:", error);
588	    }

806	## Scheduling vs Queue vs Workflows
807	
808	| Feature            | Queue              | Scheduling        | Workflows           |
809	| ------------------ | ------------------ | ----------------- | ------------------- |
810	| **When**           | Immediately (FIFO) | Future time       | Future time         |
811	| **Execution**      | Sequential         | At scheduled time | Multi-step          |
812	| **Retries**        | Automatic          | Automatic         | Automatic           |
813	| **Persistence**    | SQLite             | SQLite            | Workflow engine     |
814	| **Recurring**      | No                 | Yes (cron)        | No (use scheduling) |
815	| **Complex logic**  | No                 | No                | Yes                 |
816	| **Human approval** | No                 | No                | Yes                 |
817	
818	**Use Queue when:**
819	
820	- You need background processing without blocking the response
821	- Tasks should run ASAP but don't need to block
822	- Order matters (FIFO)
823	
824	**Use Scheduling when:**
825	
826	- Tasks need to run at a specific time
827	- You need recurring jobs (cron)
828	- Delayed execution (debouncing, retries)
829	
830	**Use Workflows when:**
831	
832	- Multi-step processes with dependencies
833	- Automatic retries with backoff
834	- Human-in-the-loop approvals
835	- Long-running tasks (minutes to hours)

837	## API Reference
838	
839	Two surfaces share these semantics: the experimental `Scheduler` primitive
840	(`agents/schedules`, methods on the scheduler instance) and the stable `Agent`
841	methods (on the Agent class, delegating to `this.scheduler`).

843	### Scheduler primitive
844	
845	#### `new Scheduler(options?)`
846	
847	```typescript
848	new Scheduler({
849	  callbacks?,
850	  retry?,
851	  hungScheduleTimeoutSeconds?,
852	  onError?
853	});
854	```

856	- `callbacks` registers scheduled callbacks by name. `set()` and `every()`
857	  type both the name and the payload against this map, and dispatch runs the
858	  registered function — the typed scheduling surface and the runtime dispatch
859	  target are the same object.
860	- Lifecycle supplies storage, readiness, startup state, alarm coordination,
861	  the host invocation boundary, events, and routing.
862	- `retry` supplies callback retry defaults. The defaults are three attempts,
863	  100 ms base delay, and 3,000 ms maximum delay.

865	- `onError` observes terminal callback failures outside ambient host context.

867	Install the constructed object with `Lifecycle.use()` before use. Scheduler

913	#### schedule()
914	
915	```typescript

917	  when: Date | string | number,
918	  callback: keyof this,
919	  payload?: T,
920	  options?: { retry?: RetryOptions; idempotent?: boolean }
921	): Promise<Schedule<T>>

924	Schedule a task for future execution.
925	
926	**Parameters:**
927	
928	- `when` - When to execute: `number` (seconds delay), `Date` (specific time), or `string` (cron expression)
929	- `callback` - Name of the method to call
930	- `payload` - Data to pass to the callback (must be JSON-serializable)
931	- `options.retry` - Optional retry configuration. See [Retries](./retries.md) for details.
932	- `options.idempotent` - Deduplicate by callback + payload. Defaults to `true` for cron schedules, `false` for delayed and Date-based schedules.

936	**Idempotency:**
937	
938	Cron schedules are idempotent by default — calling `schedule("0 * * * *", "tick")` multiple times with the same callback, cron expression, and payload returns the existing schedule instead of creating a duplicate. Set `idempotent: false` to override this.
939	
940	For delayed and Date-based schedules, set `idempotent: true` to opt in to the same dedup behavior (matched on callback + payload). This is especially useful when calling `schedule()` in `onStart()` to avoid accumulating duplicate rows across Durable Object restarts:

953	```typescript

955	  intervalSeconds: number,
956	  callback: keyof this,
957	  payload?: T,
958	  options?: { retry?: RetryOptions }
959	): Promise<Schedule<T>>
960	```
961	
962	Schedule a task to run repeatedly at a fixed interval. Idempotent by design

964	
965	**Parameters:**
966	
967	- `intervalSeconds` - Number of seconds between executions (must be > 0)
968	- `callback` - Name of the method to call
969	- `payload` - Data to pass to the callback (must be JSON-serializable)
970	- `options.retry` - Optional retry configuration. See [Retries](./retries.md) for details.

972	**Returns:** A `Schedule` object with `type: "interval"`

974	**Behavior:**
975	
976	- **Idempotent on (callback, interval, payload)** — calling with the same callback, interval, and payload returns the existing schedule instead of creating a duplicate. A different interval or payload creates a new, independent schedule.
977	- First execution occurs after `intervalSeconds` (not immediately)
978	- If callback is still running when next execution is due, it's skipped (overlap prevention)

1031	
1032	```typescript

1034	```
1035	
1036	Create an alarm-backed heartbeat that prevents the Durable Object from being evicted due to inactivity. Returns a disposer function that cancels the heartbeat when called. The disposer is idempotent — calling it multiple times is safe.
1037	
1038	See [Keeping the Agent Alive](#keeping-the-agent-alive) for usage details.

1044	```
1045	
1046	Run an async function while keeping the Durable Object alive. The heartbeat is automatically started before the function runs and stopped when it completes (whether it succeeds or throws). Returns the value returned by the function.
1047

1049	
1050	## Limits
1051	
1052	- **Maximum tasks:** Limited by SQLite storage (each task is a row). Practical limit is tens of thousands per agent.
1053	- **Task size:** Each task (including payload) can be up to 2MB.
1054	- **Minimum delay:** 0 seconds (runs on next alarm tick)
1055	- **Cron precision:** Minute-level (not seconds)
1056	- **Interval precision:** Second-level
1057	- **Cron jobs:** After execution, automatically rescheduled for the next occurrence
1058	- **Interval jobs:** After execution, rescheduled for `now + intervalSeconds`; skipped if still running

### Two wires

The client chooses how frames travel:

- **`cf-websocket`** (default) — accepted with Cloudflare's WebSocket Hibernation
  API. Idle clients remain connected while the Durable Object leaves memory;
  when a message wakes it, the constructor and lifecycle startup run again
  before `onMessage`. State needed after a wake belongs in storage or
  `connection.setState()`.
- **Cap'n Web** (`?__agents_transport=capnweb`, or
  `useAgent({ transport: "capnweb" })`) — protocol frames travel through one
  pipe method on a Cap'n Web session whose root also carries the host's
  `callables` natively. The connection is an in-memory socket and does not
  hibernate: the object stays pinned while it is open, and clients reconnect
  after an eviction.

Handlers are wire-agnostic. Both kinds of connection dispatch the same
`onConnect`/`onMessage`/`onClose`/`onError`, appear in `getConnections()`,
and honour `connection.close(code, reason)`.

## Native RPC

Native Durable Object RPC does not pass through `fetch`. An RPC method that
requires initialized capabilities starts the lifecycle explicitly:

```ts
async runTask(): Promise<void> {
  await this.lifecycle.start();
  // initialized work
}
```

An `Agent` enforces this boundary for you. Its internal RPC entry points and
the public `async` methods your subclass exposes over RPC start the lifecycle
before they run, so a cold instance does not serve those calls against
uninitialized state. Synchronous methods are never deferred; if one reads state
that `onStart` sets up, make it `async` or call `await this.lifecycle.start()`
in it. Concurrent calls to `start()` share the same startup operation, and
`lifecycle.isStarted()` returns `true` only after capabilities and `onStart()`
have finished.

Startup resolves the Durable Object name. An async RPC to an Agent addressed
with `newUniqueId()` or `idFromString()` fails instead of running before
initialization. Address the Agent by name with `getAgentByName()`, `getByName()`,
or `idFromName()`.

## Object names

Use `idFromName()` or `getByName()`. The lifecycle reads the authoritative name
from `ctx.id.name` and exposes it as `lifecycle.name`.

For migration only, the lifecycle can read an existing `__ps_name` record
written by an older PartyServer release. It never writes that key. Deprecated
name headers and bootstrap methods are not supported.

If a name cannot be resolved, the error covers named addressing, updating local
